newsitem.title: UK: New UK opposition chief faces Blair in parliament.
newsitem.headline: New UK opposition chief faces Blair in parliament.

text.p: Cartoonists depict him as a boy straining to peer over the table in the centre of the House of Commons at his rival, Prime Minister Tony Blair, but William Hague survived his parliamentary baptism of fire unscathed as the new leader of Britain's Conservatives on Wednesday.
Yet the image of a young boy in short trousers lingered, reinforced by the presence of two of his predecessors as Hague faced Blair at his first Prime Minister's Question Time as party leader.

Slouched just a couple of feet away, former Conservative prime minister Edward Heath glowered across at Blair as he has done since Labour was swept into power in a landslide on May 1. The 1970s-era leader showed no sign he was aware of Hague's takeover.
But, three benches behind the prematurely balding 36-year-old Hague, his immediate predecessor as Conservative leader, John Major, nodded in approval as Hague battled to best Blair.

Hague's ordeal began in true British parliamentary tradition --- with insults. As the compact Hague stood to speak after a question whether Britain's beer drinkers were being given short measures when they ordered a pint in pubs, Labour MPs aunted him with cries of "half pint".

But Hague, former Welsh Secretary, ploughed on, quizzing Blair about reports that a Welsh MP had been threatened with expulsion from the party for saying he would campaign against Labour's election promise of a referendum for a Welsh assembly.
If anyone expected fireworks, they were disappointed.
Blair, at 44 closer in age to Hague than he was to the 54-year-old former prime minister Major, looked assured, dismissing the new opposition leader's questions as based on incorrect media reports.

Hague, aware that with Blair's majority of 179 he faces a marathon rather than a sprint before he comes close to power, made a debut that was firm but measured -- earning respect, but not unqualified praise, from columnists watching the exchanges.
But at least one person seemed pleased.

As Blair batted away a biting question with a quip that Hague had prepared it before listening to the earlier answer, Major smiled wistfully and whispered audibly to his neighbour, Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble: "That's my line."
Hague's questions over, Major scribbled a note and sent it snaking from hand to hand down to Hague.

Nodding vigorously, Hague tucked the note into his pocket, not even turning round to acknowledge the man who spent six years facing questions in the House of Commons twice a week for seven years -- an ordeal Major said he hated.

On Wednesday Major looked strikingly different from the way he was when he faced Blair across the Commons chamber as prime minister. Blair and Hague have inherited his dogged determination. Major just oozed relief.
